summary: Describes the changes to OSPF needed to support IPv6. The fundamental mechanisms, including flooding, designated router election, areas, and SPF calculations, stay the same. Changes were needed because of differences in protocol semantics between IPv4 and IPv6 and to handle the larger addresses. It replaced RFC 2740 and has been updated several times.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the routing system for the newer, longer internet addresses. It works like the older version, with small changes to fit the longer addresses.

questions: how does ospf work with ipv6
what is a link lsa in ospfv3
subtitle: OSPF version 3: the same link-state routing engine, reworked to carry IPv6 prefixes.

tldr.problem: OSPF for IPv4 bakes IPv4 addressing into its packets, LSAs and neighbor logic, so it cannot simply carry IPv6 routes.
tldr.mechanism: OSPFv3 keeps flooding, Designated Router election, areas and SPF, but strips addresses out of packets and the core LSAs, runs per link instead of per subnet, adds new LSA types for IPv6 prefixes, and leaves authentication to IPsec.
tldr.outcome: It became the OSPF for IPv6 specification, replacing RFC 2740. It has since been updated by RFC 6845, RFC 6860, RFC 7503, RFC 8362 and RFC 9454.

today: RFC 5340 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2740. It has not been obsoleted but has been updated by RFC 6845, RFC 6860, RFC 7503, RFC 8362 and RFC 9454, so read it together with those updates.

sections.title: OSPF for IPv6 in Brief
sections.content:
OSPF for IPv6, also called OSPFv3, describes the changes needed to run OSPF over IPv6. The fundamental mechanisms are unchanged: flooding, Designated Router (DR) election, area support and Shortest Path First (SPF) calculation. Changes were needed either because protocol semantics differ between IPv4 and IPv6 or simply to handle the larger addresses, and they require the protocol version to go from 2 to 3.

Neighbor discovery with Hello packets, adjacency formation, the interface and neighbor state machines, the link types (point-to-point, broadcast, NBMA, point-to-multipoint and virtual links) and LSA aging all stay as they were in OSPF version 2 (RFC 2328). OSPFv3 runs directly over IPv6 and supports the optional capabilities of OSPF for IPv4, including demand circuits and Not-So-Stubby Areas (NSSAs).
sections.plainLanguage: Routers still say hello, pick a leader, and share news with each other the same way. Only the address part changed to fit the longer addresses.

sections.title: What Changed from OSPF for IPv4
sections.content:
The RFC groups the differences into several themes.

  • Per link, not per subnet. IPv6 allows several prefixes on one link, and two nodes can talk without sharing a prefix, so OSPF now runs per link.
  • No addressing in the core. IPv6 addresses appear only in LSA payloads. Router IDs, Area IDs and Link State IDs stay 32 bits and can no longer be assigned as IPv6 addresses. Neighbors are always identified by Router ID.
  • Flooding scope. The LS type now says whether an LSA is link-local, area-wide or AS-wide.
  • Instance ID. Several OSPF instances can run on one link, for example when providers share a segment.
  • Link-local addresses. OSPF packets are sent from the interface's link-local address, except on virtual links, which MUST use a global address. Link-local addresses MUST NOT be advertised in inter-area-prefix, AS-external, NSSA or intra-area-prefix LSAs.
  • Authentication removed. The AuType and Authentication fields are gone from the header.

The Options field grows to 24 bits, and a prefix is now expressed as a prefix plus length instead of an address and mask. The default route is a prefix of length 0. The Router ID 0.0.0.0 is reserved and SHOULD NOT be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rules mixed street names into every message. Now the messages say only who is next to whom, and a separate note lists which streets belong where.

sections.title: Packets and the Hello
sections.content:
OSPFv3 packets travel directly in IPv6 with Next Header value 89. There are five packet types, all starting with a standard 16-byte header: Hello, Database Description, Link State Request, Link State Update and Link State Acknowledgment. The header holds version 3, the type, packet length, Router ID, Area ID, an IPv6 upper-layer checksum and the Instance ID. Received packets with a different Instance ID than the interface are discarded.

Hello packets are sent to the multicast address FF02::5 (AllSPFRouters), and some flooding packets also go to FF02::6 (AllDRouters). These are link-local scope and the Hop Limit should be 1. The Hello now carries an Interface ID instead of a network mask, plus the router priority, Options, HelloInterval, RouterDeadInterval, and the DR and Backup DR identified by Router ID (0.0.0.0 if none yet).

Routers on a link must agree on HelloInterval and RouterDeadInterval, or they will not form neighbor relationships. The RFC also says OSPFv3 packets SHOULD be sent with DSCP CS6 where routers map the IPv6 Traffic Class to DSCP.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers shout hello to the neighbors on the same street, saying their own ID number and who they think is the leader. If the hello settings do not match, they do not become friends.

sections.title: Link State Advertisements
sections.content:
Every LSA begins with a 20-byte header. The 16-bit LS type has a U bit that says how to treat an unknown type (0: treat as link-local; 1: store and flood anyway) and two scope bits S2 and S1 (link-local, area, AS, or reserved), followed by a function code.

The router-LSA and network-LSA now carry only topology, so the router's interface information may be split across several router-LSAs that receivers must combine. Prefixes live elsewhere. Intra-area-prefix-LSAs attach prefixes to a router-LSA or network-LSA. Inter-area-prefix-LSAs and inter-area-router-LSAs are the old type 3 and type 4 summary LSAs. AS-external-LSAs and NSSA-LSAs carry external prefixes, with optional forwarding address and route tag.

The new link-LSA never leaves the link. It tells neighbors the router's link-local address, the prefixes on the link, and Options bits for the network-LSA. For network-LSAs and link-LSAs the Link State ID is the originator's Interface ID. The DR sets the network-LSA Options to the logical OR of the link-LSAs from its fully adjacent neighbors.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers write little notes about their surroundings. Some notes stay on the street (link), some go around the neighborhood (area), and a few go to the whole town (AS).

sections.title: Flooding and Route Calculation
sections.content:
Most flooding rules are as in OSPFv2, but the interfaces eligible for flooding an LSA now depend on its scope. AS-scoped LSAs go out all interfaces except virtual links, and AS-external-LSAs are not flooded into stub or NSSA areas. An unknown LSA with U bit 0 is treated as link-local, while with U bit 1 it is stored and flooded as if understood. A self-originated LSA is simply one whose Advertising Router is the router's own Router ID.

The SPF calculation follows the five steps of OSPFv2. The graph's vertices are routers (named by Router ID) and transit links (named by the DR's Interface ID plus its Router ID). Instead of reading stub networks out of router-LSAs, the router reads the area's intra-area-prefix-LSAs, and the cost of a prefix is its metric plus the cost to the referenced router or transit link.

Next hops are link-local addresses taken from the neighbor's link-LSA, which is needed on links such as NBMA where routers need not exchange Hellos. Virtual links must use global addresses, and AS-scoped LSAs are never flooded over them.
sections.plainLanguage: A note is passed only as far as its label says. Each router then works out the shortest paths on its map, and adds the street lists from the notes to find the way to each address.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 2740
sections.content:
RFC 5340 obsoletes RFC 2740. Implementations of RFC 2740 fully interoperate with this specification, and all the additions and changes are backward compatible.

  • Support for multiple interfaces on the same link, only partly specified before, is now spelled out. One Active Interface sends and receives OSPF control traffic and the others become Standby, with a new Standby interface state.
  • MOSPF (multicast extensions) for IPv6 is deprecated. The RFC says there are no known implementations.
  • An NSSA specification unique to OSPFv3 is included.
  • The stub area restriction on flooding unknown LSAs is deprecated, so link and area scope LSAs with U bit 1 now flood through stub and NSSA areas.
  • A LinkLSASuppression interface parameter allows suppressing link-LSAs on interfaces that are not broadcast or NBMA.
  • The DN-bit is added to the prefix options, and all references to site-local addresses are removed.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the updated rulebook. Players using the old rulebook can still play with players using the new one.

sections.title: Authentication and Security
sections.content:
OSPFv3 has no authentication of its own. It relies on the IP Authentication Header (RFC 4302) and the IP Encapsulating Security Payload (RFC 4303), as described in RFC 4552, for integrity and authentication or confidentiality. The standard IPv6 checksum only protects against accidental corruption.

When IPsec is used, an implementation must check the Security Association and the local SA database so that a packet authenticated with an SA defined for another protocol on the same system is not accepted as OSPFv3. The mechanisms do not protect against compromised, malfunctioning or misconfigured routers, which can disrupt a whole routing domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The routing game does not lock its own messages. It borrows the internet's lock and key system, and that still cannot stop a router that is itself broken or dishonest.

items.desc: Asks for more recent pieces of the neighbor's database.

fields.desc: Seconds since the LSA was originated.

fields.desc: U and scope bits plus the LSA function code.

items.label: Router-LSA
items.desc: Area scope. Describes a router's interfaces to the area.

items.label: Network-LSA
items.desc: Area scope. Originated by the DR; lists routers on the link.

items.label: Inter-Area-Prefix-LSA
items.desc: Area scope. A prefix outside the area but inside the AS.

items.label: Inter-Area-Router-LSA
items.desc: Area scope. A path to an AS boundary router.

items.label: AS-External-LSA
items.desc: AS scope. A prefix outside the AS.

items.label: Deprecated
items.desc: Previously used by MOSPF; may be reassigned.

items.label: NSSA-LSA
items.desc: Area scope. External prefix limited to one NSSA.

items.label: Link-LSA
items.desc: Link-local scope. Link-local address and prefixes of the link.

items.label: Intra-Area-Prefix-LSA
items.desc: Area scope. Prefixes tied to a router-LSA or network-LSA.
